story.title: Mira and the Snack Cart
story.thread: Mira packs snack boxes for the school fair. Her little red train carries each box to a new stop. At every stop she compares two groups, then chuffs onward.
story.opening: Mira turns the little red train toward the school fair. Her snack cart is full, and every box has a comparing job.
story.closing: The last box is packed. Mira waves from the red train because every stop helped her compare two groups with care.

beats.narration: First stop, Apple Orchard. Mira counts two apples and three bananas. Which group comes first?
Next stop, Ribbon Bridge. Mira ties three red ribbons and five blue ones. Both counts can grow together.
Last stop, Bead Garden. Mira shares beads between friend boxes. Each part must get its fair count.

concepts.title: What a ratio compares
concepts.narration: At Apple Orchard, Mira learns that a ratio names two groups in a chosen order.

practiceQuestions.stem: Mira packs 2 apple boxes and 3 banana boxes. Which ratio compares apples to bananas?
practiceQuestions.hint: Apples are named first, so their count goes first.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Apples come first in the question: 2 apples to 3 bananas is 2 : 3.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Ask the child to point to the apple group before choosing.
misconceptions: Reversing the order of the two groups

practiceQuestions.stem: A bowl has 4 red berries and 1 yellow berry. Which ratio is red to yellow?
practiceQuestions.hint: The red group is named first in the question.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Red berries are named first: 4 red to 1 yellow is 4 : 1.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Let the child say both group names aloud before revealing.
misconceptions: Mixing the part ratio with the total

practiceQuestions.stem: Mira's red train has 3 red carriages and 2 blue carriages. Which ratio is blue to red?
practiceQuestions.hint: Blue is asked first, so 2 comes before 3.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Blue to red puts the 2 blue carriages before the 3 red carriages.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Cover the word order, then ask which group should be written first.
misconceptions: Using red to blue instead of blue to red

concepts.title: Equivalent ratios
concepts.narration: At Ribbon Bridge, Mira sees that multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the comparison the same.

practiceQuestions.hint: Multiply both parts of 3 : 5 by the same number.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 3 × 2 = 6 and 5 × 2 = 10, so 6 : 10 keeps the same comparison.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Draw two matching jumps, one for each part of the ratio.

practiceQuestions.stem: Mira uses 2 red strips and 4 blue strips. Which ratio matches this comparison?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2 : 4 has the same comparison as 1 : 2 because both parts were halved.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Ask what happens when both piles are split into two equal groups.
misconceptions: Using the total 6 as one part

practiceQuestions.stem: Mira doubles the ratio 4 : 7. Which new ratio does she get?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 4 × 2 = 8 and 7 × 2 = 14, so the matching ratio is 8 : 14.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Check that the child multiplies both parts, not only one.

concepts.title: Sharing in a ratio
concepts.narration: At Bead Garden, Mira turns a ratio into equal-sized parts so every friend box gets the right share.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 3 : 5 ribbon has a shorter piece of 12 cm. How long is the longer piece?
practiceQuestions.explanation: One part is 4 cm, so the longer 5-part piece is 20 cm.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Sketch three short boxes and five matching boxes on the board.
misconceptions: Using 5 ÷ 3 instead of a shared part value

practiceQuestions.stem: Red : blue beads are 4 : 7. There are 44 beads in all. How many are blue?
practiceQuestions.hint: There are 11 equal parts in the whole group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 44 ÷ 11 = 4 beads per part, and blue has 7 parts, so 7 × 4 = 28.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Have the child count the parts before choosing an option.
misconceptions: Treating 7 as a share count rather than a part count

practiceQuestions.stem: Mira splits 30 snacks in a 2 : 3 ratio. What is the bigger share?
practiceQuestions.hint: There are 5 equal parts in 30 snacks.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each part is 6 snacks, and the bigger 3-part share is 18.
practiceQuestions.trainerInstructions: Ask which number in 2 : 3 names the bigger group before calculating.
misconceptions: Giving the smaller share as the answer

completionRule.narrationContinuity: One Mira snack-cart story runs from Apple Orchard to Ribbon Bridge to Bead Garden.
